body: Intro · resources · crops & horticulture
Grade 11 is the *foundation* year before Grade 12 livestock/forest/soil-water/management. Three units. Flip cards and a quiz after each unit.

units.title: Introduction to Agriculture
units.intro: Agriculture is the science and art of growing plants and raising animals for food, fibre, fuel and income. It is how societies eat — and in Eritrea it is still the main livelihood.

cards.title: A short history you can tell in four beats · 1 Hunting–gathering
body: Wild food only. No fields.

cards.title: 2 Domestication
body: Cereals, pulses, sheep and goats first. Settled villages.

cards.title: 3 Traditional farming
body: Ox plough, local seed, rain-fed, mixed livestock.

cards.title: 4 Science + tech
body: Improved seed, fertiliser, irrigation, extension — used carefully so soil still lives.

cards.title: Mnemonic — H.D.T.S.
body: *Hunt, Domesticate, Tradition, Science.* If an exam asks “stages of agricultural development”, walk those four, then add the Eritrean present: mostly rain-fed smallholders plus some irrigation schemes.

cards.title: 1.1.1 From Gatherings and Hunting towards Crop Rotation and Livestock Production
body: Where and when agriculture began is not known as people in different places in the world cultivated crops and reared animals.
Early peoples began by hunting and fishing and by gathering fruits, leaves, bark and honey.
Private ownership of property was almost unknown, although competition for scarce or highly appreciated food sources already existed.
One effect of this early form of agriculture was that people started to store surplus production for use in lean times.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which traditional land-holding system, characterized by rotational village land redistribution every $$5\text{ to }7\text{ years}$$, historically discouraged long-term agricultural soil investments?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
The *dessa* system was a communal land tenure system where land belonged to the village and was redistributed every $$5\text{ to }7\text{ years}$$. Since farmers did not have permanent ownership, they lacked incentives to build long-term soil conservation structures.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the system is **Dessa**.

steps.text: Sand feels gritty and will not ribbon; silt feels smooth; clay ribbons and sticks.

cards.title: Roles of agriculture
body: Food security, raw materials (cotton, hides), jobs, export earnings, rural life, manure that returns to the field. Weak agriculture → people leave the land and cities swell.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Food Supply
body: The Eritrean agricultural sector produces a wide range and quantity of quality foods.
Common cereals include wheat, barley, sorghum, pearl millet, finger millet and taff.
Oil crops include cottonseed, sesame, groundnut, Niger seed and linseed.
Fruits include bananas, oranges, lemons, mangos, guavas, apples, etc.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Source of Income
body: Agriculture is a source of income from sales of agricultural products such as fruits, vegetables, grains, oil seeds, cotton, live animals (cattle, sheep, goats, poultry) and animal products (hides and skins, milk, butter, honey, etc.).

cards.title: 1.2.3 Earners of Foreign Currency
body: Exports of agricultural products are a major source of foreign currency.

The foreign currency earned could be used for importing various such as petroleum products, agricultural machineries, electronic equipment medicine, and fertilizers, which are not produced within the country.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Raw Materials
body: Agriculture is the basis of the development of agriculture-based industries such as the food-processing, textile, leather, brewery and sugar industries.
Wheat and other grains are used in the manufacturing of flour and pasta.
Malting barley is used for the manufacture of beer.
Sugar is processed from sugar cane and sugar beet.

cards.title: 1.2.5 Employment
body: Agriculture is the most important sector of the Eritrean rural economy and the main source of livelihood.
Dairy, poultry and horticultural farms, which produce fruits and vegetables, employ large amounts of labour.
Many people are also employed in the processing, packing, distribution and marketing of agricultural products.
Agriculture-related industries such as seed-processing, fertilizer, pesticides, herbicides, pharmaceutics and agricultural machinery are also sources of employment.

cards.title: 1.2.6 Source of Fuel
body: Domestic energy sources such as wood, charcoal, dung, etc. are obtained from agriculture.
Wood is obtained from forests and woodlands.
Animal dung is used as a source of fuel.
Animal manure is used to produce biogas that can be used for fuel.

cards.title: 1.2.7 Socio-cultural Heritage
body: The role agriculture plays in socio-cultural heritage is easily recognizable in livestock production systems.
Livestock serve important social purposes for example as a form of insurance or banking for the majority of people living in rural areas.
The prestige associated with the type of animal owned may vary from one area to another.
In Eritrea a farmer who owns a large number of animals commands greater community respect than those who don’t.

cards.title: 1.2.8 Environmental Impact
body: Agriculture has a significant impact on the environment that can either be positive or negative.
Afforestation, land reclamation, the appropriate use of animal manure as fertilizer and the pollination activities of bees are positive effects agricultural activities have on the environment.

cards.title: 1.2.9 Source of Energy
body: Livestock play a major role in supplying energy for ploughing, transport, water carrying, etc. thus contributing to reducing the amount of human labour required and contributing significantly to the economy of the country.

cards.title: 1.2.10 Source of Construction Materials
body: The agricultural sector generates materials for the construction of various forms of shelter.
Wood for example is used in the construction of houses, in making furniture and to provide fencing poles.
Straw from sorghum and pearl millet are used for fencing, for house construction and for roofing..

body: A farming system is a system in which various components or elements of a farm are interlinked in various ways.
The linkages are draught, feed, manure, capital, social, etc.
Agriculture in Eritrea has remained at subsistence level for several generations.
Subsistence or small-scale farmers and agropastoralists manage approximately 95 per cent of the cultivated land in the country.
A small number of farmers concentrate on commercial production using modern technologies.

cards.title: Constraints (why yields stay low)
body: Erratic rain and drought, thin eroded soils, small fragmented plots, pests, weak seed and input supply, limited credit, labour peaks at weeding/harvest, land degradation. Development means attacking several of these at once — a new variety alone is not enough if the terrace is gone.

cards.title: 1.4.1 Natural Factors
body: Based on the origin of the constraint, the major limiting factors can be divided into three major broad categories: natural (biotic or abiotic), anthropogenic and socio-economic factors.
Different types of insect, disease and weed affect production.
The type of insect, disease and weed differ from one area to another.
Bacteria, fungi and viruses cause most of the common diseases in Eritrea that affect crops and livestock.

cards.title: 1.4.2 Anthropogenic Factors
body: Degraded land will be less productive even if improved technology and management is applied and climatic conditions become more favourable.

The effects of land degradation are decreased productivity of a unit land per specified input, a decline in livestock population, a loss of vegetation cover and a shortage of fuel wood and wood materials, a loss of topsoil, and general ecological disruption.
Land degradation is caused by overgrazing, over-cultivation and deforestation.
Significant areas of forest and woodland have been consumed to meet the demands of wood for fuel, building materials and the expansion of land for cultivation.

cards.title: 1.4.3 Socio-economic Factors
body: The most important socio-economic factors affecting agricultural production in Eritrea are: poor marketing and storage facilities, inadequate agricultural inputs, poor infrastructure, poor awareness, the effects of war and insufficient technical inputs.
Farmers do not have free access to credit and loans.
Information on prices of agricultural produce is also almost non-existent.
Most agricultural products are by nature perishable.

2.1.1 Temperature
body: Temperature is one of the most important climatic factors affecting the distribution and abundance of plants and animals.
Temperature is a significant factor as both low and high temperature ranges limit plant and animal growth and development.
Several parameters are used to delineate and describe geographical areas within the same climate.
Isotherms (e.g. the yearly isotherms) are the lines connecting the locations with the same mean yearly temperature of 20 °C or a yearly isotherm of 25 °C.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Relative Humidity
body: Relative humidity is the measure of the amount of atmospheric moisture in relation to saturated air.
Temperature also affects relative humidity.
Explain the importance of light for a plant.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Rainfall
body: Water is essential for all crops and livestock and forms an integral part of all living systems.
Water is important because it is a major force in shaping climatic patterns.
Water stress can vary in degree from a small decrease in water potential to a lethal limit of desiccation.
Temperature and precipitation act together to affect the physiological and ecological status of plants.

cards.title: 2.1.4 Solar Radiation
body: Solar radiation consists of a range of electromagnetic spectra including radiowaves, ultraviolet (UV) rays, visible light, X-rays and gamma rays.
The components have different level of energy.
When electromagnetic energy is strikes any given surface, three fundamental energy interactions are possible: reflection, absorption and transmission.
A fraction of the radiant energy is reflected, absorbed and/or transmitted.

cards.title: 2.1.5 Light
body: Changes in day length or photoperiod regulate the phenological development (germination up to seed setting) of crops and rangelands.

cards.title: 2.1.6 Topography
body: Topography refers to a relief feature of land.
Topography determines the amount of light absorbed, wind speed, direction and rainfall.
Soils on slopes and hilltops are eroded and deposited in the valleys, hence, the soils in the valleys are richer and deeper than those on the slopes.
Because of this, these lands are generally suitable for cultivation.

body: Weathering is the chemical alteration and physical breakdown of rocks during exposure to the atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere.
A soil profile is the vertical cross-sectional view of the soil through all its horizons extending into the parent material.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Soil Profile Description
body: Soils developed from sandy parent materials will rapidly show a mature soil profile because they contain few soluble materials.
Clay soils are slower in their drainage capacity and are, therefore, slower to develop a fully mature soil profile.
The master horizons are denoted by O, A, B and C.
Examples include beach sand, windblown silt, alluvium deposited by rivers, etc.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Soil Composition
body: Soil phases are regions inside a system, which are internally physically uniform.
The solid phase constitutes the soil matrix, which is the combination of solids and pores in a soil.
Water and air make-up the liquid and gas parts of the soil; the gaseous phase is the soil atmosphere.
Soil is rather like a big sponge containing numerous tiny pores that wind through its structure.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Soil Properties
body: Soil is a unique material with its own physical, chemical and biological properties.
Physical properties of soil include: soil texture, soil structure, soil consistency, the soil liquid phase, soil gases and others (temperature, depth, colour).
Quantitatively, soil texture is the measure of the distribution of particle sizes or the proportion of the various size ranges of particles.
Based on particle size, there are three broad groups of soil textural classes.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Methods of Soil Texture Determination

In silt loam, it form aggregates with some level of roughness.

cards.title: 2.2.6 Soil Structure
body: Soil structure refers to the grouping or arrangement of primary particles into secondary units or peds/aggregates.
The units are characterized and classified based on size, shape and degree of distinctness.
Presence of organic matter and inorganic cation such as Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe3+ and Al3+ promote flocculation (binding) of aggregates and aggregate stability.
The presence of sodium disperses or separates aggregates and the soil becomes unstable aggregates.

cards.title: 2.2.7 Measurement Techniques for Soil-water and Soil-water Potentials
body: Soil-water content can be measured directly and indirectly in the field and laboratory.
Among the techniques used are the gravimetric (weighing or direct) method.
Likewise, neutron scattering uses a neutron probe directly to measure the soil-water relations in the field.
The result in the example shows that the soil moisture is adequate for plant growth.

cards.title: 2.2.8 Soil-water Potential
body: Soil-water potential can be measured in the field by using tensiometers (0.0–0.8 bar) or in the laboratory with a tension plate (usually up to 0.8 bar) and a pressure plate (from 1–100 bars).
Saturated movement of water occurs when the soil pores are filled or saturated with water.
Unsaturated soil-water movement occurs, when the pores are partially filled with water.

Vapour movement of water is a movement in the form of vapour, which occurs both internally within the soil pores and externally on the land by surface-by-surface evaporation because of a vapour pressure differential.

cards.title: 2.2.9 The Soil Gaseous Phase
body: Soil aeration expresses the rate of gas exchange between soil air and the atmosphere.
Soil aeration controls the level of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the soil.
Air can move into the soil only once water has drained out of the pores.
Carbon dioxide content is sometimes 5–10 times higher than the atmospheric carbon dioxide content and may even reach 10 per cent.

cards.title: 2.2.10 Other Physical Properties of Soil
body: Generally, dark soil surfaces will absorb more heat than light surfaces.
Losses of absorbed heat occur by radiation back into the atmosphere as long-wave radiation, heating the air and cooling the soil.
Farmers in Eritrea cover seedbeds with stubble, grasses and tree branches in order to facilitate germination of seeds.
Reddish-brown colours indicate well-drained soils.

The most important chemical properties of soil include: soil colloid, soil reaction (acidity and alkalinity), salinity.
Colloids can hold ions because they have an overall negative (−) or positive (+) charge on their surfaces, depending upon the chemical structure and soil pH conditions.
Humus has a complex chemical composition consisting mainly of C, H and O, and smaller amounts of S, P and N, among others.

In the classification of salt-affected soils, a saline soil has high soluble salts ($$EC_{se} > 4\text{ dS/m}$$), but low exchangeable sodium ($$ESP < 15\%$$\) and a moderate pH ($$pH < 8.5$$\). Sodic and saline-sodic soils have an ESP greater than $$15\%$$.

**Conclusion**
This soil is classified as **Saline**.

cards.q: What is the recommended chemical amendment used to reclaim sodic soils by supplying Calcium ($$Ca^{2+}$$) to displace exchangeable Sodium ($$Na^+$$)?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Gypsum ($$CaSO_4$$) is highly effective for sodic soil reclamation. It dissolves to supply $$Ca^{2+}$$ ions, which replace the exchangeable $$Na^+$$ on clay colloid surfaces. The displaced $$Na^+$$ is then washed out as soluble $$Na_2SO_4$$.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct amendment is **Gypsum**.

Indirectly, the water present in the soil helps the plant in many ways.

Soil air or oxygen is useful in increasing the nutrientavailability of the soil by breaking down the insoluble minerals into soluble salts; decomposing plant and animal remains and bringing about nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing processes by bacteria.

cards.title: The season in order — never skip a step on the paper
body:
- **Site:** depth, slope, previous crop, water, access.
- **Land prep:** plough/hoe to a fine enough tilth, on contour if sloped, bury residues or compost.
- **Fertiliser:** organic (manure, compost) feeds soil life; mineral NPK corrects a measured shortage. Split nitrogen so rain does not wash it all at once.
- **Sowing:** right date (rain), depth, rate, method — broadcasting, drilling/rows, transplanting for some horticulture.
- **Protection:** weeds steal light and water; insects and diseases need scouting + resistant varieties + sanitation + only then chemicals if available and safe.

Favourable climate and adequate water supply are required for optimal production.

body: Land preparation is a requirement for crop production.
The timing and the quality of land preparation influence the growth of crops.
Poor and untimely land preparation may cause serious weed problems and may lead to soil erosion.
Physical loosening of the soil can be carried out in a range of cultivation operations by hand, animaldrawn ploughs or machines.

body: Plants cannot live without the 16 essential elements.
Plants obtain these nutritional elements from the soil.
If the soil is deficient in any of these elements due to natural conditions, leaching or intensive crop cultivation, they must be replaced in with fertilizer.
Examples of inorganic fertilizers are: urea and di-ammonium phosphate (DAP).

cards.title: 3.3.4 Sowing
body: Sowing of crops is influenced by the nature of the precipitation, temperature, occurrence of diseases and pests as well as marketing.
On a seasonal basis the crop should be planted at a time when there is enough subsequent rainfall.
Planting in moist soil allows rapid seed germination or sprouting.
Under semi-arid conditions, early sowing contributes to efficient water use.

cards.title: 3.3.5 Methods of Sowing
body: Seed is sown into the soil using different mechanical planters or by hand.
Generally, three sowing methods are used: broadcasting, row planting and sowing in drills.

Row planting has an advantage because the amount of seed required is less; it is also possible carry out inter-row cultivation and spraying chemicals without damaging the plant and the yield is also better.
Under dry land conditions, farmers traditionally use high seed rates for certain crops.

Unit Three Crop Production a source of animal feed, manure or compost and have medicinal values.

Cultivation promotes nitrification in the soil, controls weeds; conserves soil moisture by preventing runoff and providing sufficient aeration.

cards.title: 3.3.8 Harvesting
body: Harvesting is the deliberate detachment of the edible or usable part of the crop for use as an agricultural product.
In modern agriculture, harvesting may include cutting, threshing of crops, separating crop from the debris, or cleaning using combined harvesters.
Premature and over-matured crops result in loss of yield quality, quantity or both.
The most common indicators for harvesting are when the crop changes its colour to brown or a yellowish colour.

Harvesting is the deliberate detachment of the edible or usable part of the crop for use as an agricultural product.
Crop rotation is a system of land-use practice in which crops are grown in sequence on the same piece of land.
Mixed cropping or inter-cropping is a system of growing two or more crops on the same land.
Horticulture is a branch of agriculture, which involves the production and handling of horticultural crops and deals with activities related to protection and maintenance of the environment.
Vegetative propagation is the use of vegetative parts such as the stem, leaf and root to reproduce plants.

similar.q: The process of joining two plants to allow them to grow as a single unit is referred to as  A) budding.  B) grafting.  C) T-budding.  D) layering.  E) transplanting.
similar.a: B. grafting. — Grafting uses a scion with two or more buds; budding (including T-budding) is a special case that uses only a single bud.
